name: Rose Taupe
lede: Rose Taupe is a greyed, brownish pink, first recorded by Maerz and Paul in 1930 as a cross between the warmth of rose and the muted grey of taupe.

sections.title: Between rose and taupe
sections.body:
Our library ties Rose Taupe to Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color*, recording it as first used in 1924 and plotting it on plate 16, position A4 [1]. Taupe itself comes from the French word for mole, after the animal's grey-brown fur, so Rose Taupe names a color that leans that grey-brown tone toward pink without losing its mutedness [1]. ColorHub's ISCC-NBS mapping calls it a grayish red, a very close match at only 1.1 units from the nearest block, close to 4.2R 4.4/4.5 in Munsell notation [2]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS lists also carry several near-synonyms for the same small block of color, including Antique Rose, Appleblossom Pink and Ash Rose, all grouped within a couple of units of this hue [1].

Its closest listed library neighbor is [[mauve]], 14.1 units away, and nearby sit [[taupe]] itself and [[copper-rose|Copper Rose]], the clearest sibling in both name and hue [2]. [[dusty-rose|Dusty Rose]] sits just to the pinker side of the same family [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match to Rose Taupe in 139 of 23,781 paintings, 0.58 percent, with the within-painting test narrowing that to 57, making it more common than roughly 52 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 9 of 1,674 paintings, present in 0.5 percent of our paintings from that century, 1.9 times the expected rate, and the earliest match, as photographed, is a painting dated to the year 1000, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. Inside the paintings that carry it, the color most often plays an accent, 42 percent of the time, rather than a shadow or a highlight [3]. In printed English the phrase itself only takes off in the 1920s, which fits Maerz and Paul's 1924 date closely [4].
